Constructs two new benchmarks (Inj-SQuAD, Inj-TriviaQA) with diverse injected instructions at multiple positions, evaluates existing instructed-LLM and open-source detectors, trains custom detection models, and proposes two removal methods, a segmentation-removal approach that deletes document segments flagged as containing injections and an extraction-removal approach that trains a model to identify and excise the injected span. Combines the best detection and removal components into a unified filtering defense and shows it outperforms prior prompt-engineering (Sandwich, Instructional) and fine-tuning (StruQ) baselines on Inj-TriviaQA, while identifying persistent weaknesses around injection position and cross-attack generalization. Matters as a systematic empirical study specifically of the post-detection removal step for indirect injection, a stage prior work largely neglects in favor of detection or prevention alone.

title: PromptShield: Deployable Detection for Prompt Injection Attacks
artifacts_released: Y - benchmark on HuggingFace at https://huggingface.co/datasets/hendzh/PromptShield and source code at https://github.com/wagner-group/PromptShield
models_evaluated: Detector architectures fine-tuned and compared: DeBERTa-v3-base, FLAN-T5-small/base/large, Llama-3-2-1B-Instruct, Llama-3-1-8B-Instruct; prior detectors compared include PromptGuard and other existing prompt-injection classifiers.
datasets_benchmarks: Introduces the PromptShield benchmark, curated from Alpaca, databricks-dolly, natural-instructions and SPP instruction-following datasets plus IFEval for conversational-style benign data, combined with application-structured data and prompt injection attacks generated via multiple optimization-free injection techniques from the literature; includes a dedicated train/evaluation split and a taxonomy separating conversational data from application-structured data.
key_result: The PromptShield detector (best configuration) achieves 65.3% true positive rate at 0.1% false positive rate on the benchmark's evaluation split, versus only 9.4% TPR at the same FPR for the best prior detector (PromptGuard achieves 22.8% TPR at 2.9% FPR, dropping to 12.8% TPR when its FPR is reduced to a comparable low level); larger fine-tuned architectures (FLAN-T5-large, Llama-3.1-8B) substantially outperform smaller ones (FLAN-T5-small, Llama-3.2-1B) in the low-FPR regime, and DeBERTa-v3-base outperforms all prior schemes above 0.1% FPR.
baselines_compared: PromptGuard and other existing prompt-injection detection schemes evaluated at matched, extremely low FPR operating points (1%, 0.5%, 0.1%, 0.05%), plus an internal architecture comparison across DeBERTa, FLAN-T5 (small/base/large) and Llama-3 (1B/8B) variants fine-tuned on the same benchmark.
threat_model: An adversary who controls part of the data fed into an LLM-integrated application (e.g., a document, tool output, or user-supplied content) embeds additional instructions to subvert the application's intended behavior; the defender is a standalone detector monitoring all traffic to the LLM, which must operate under a severe base-rate imbalance (injection traffic is rare relative to benign conversational and application traffic) and therefore requires an extremely low false-positive rate to be deployable, while also distinguishing prompt injection from jailbreaks and correctly treating conversational chatbot data as essentially injection-free.
stated_limitations: The authors state their training setup does not account for concept drift or optimized adversarial attacks specifically crafted to bypass detection, so detector performance may degrade as attacker strategies evolve without ongoing adaptation (suggesting continuous learning as future work), and that the approach is limited to text-based inputs and does not extend to multi-modal prompt injection scenarios.
technical_summary: Introduces PromptShield, a benchmark and accompanying fine-tuned detector for prompt injection, motivated by the observation that prior detectors are evaluated unrealistically and fail to achieve the extremely low false-positive rates required for deployment given the large volume of benign traffic. Defines a taxonomy separating conversational chatbot data (assumed injection-free) from application-structured data (where injections occur), curates a benchmark spanning multiple instruction-following datasets and published optimization-free injection techniques with a dedicated low-FPR evaluation regime, and fine-tunes several classifier architectures on it. Shows that careful data curation plus larger models yields a detector that vastly outperforms prior schemes (including PromptGuard) specifically in the low-FPR operating range that matters for real deployment. Matters as a benchmark that reframes prompt-injection detection evaluation around realistic base rates and as a concretely stronger detection-stage defense than prior published detectors, though it targets only detection (not removal/mitigation) and is explicitly not evaluated against adaptive or optimization-based attackers.

artifacts_released: N - the paper proposes a conceptual response-design framework (Figure 1) with no implementation, code, or dataset released.

baselines_compared: None - no baseline comparison is performed since no system is built or tested.

title: An Early Categorization of Prompt Injection Attacks on Large Language Models
artifacts_released: N - no dataset, code, or systematic artifact is released; examples cited are drawn from prior literature and informal online sources, tested ad hoc rather than released as a benchmark.
models_evaluated: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5/GPT-4-backed), GPT-3, Bing Chat/Bing AI (GPT-4-backed), Google Bard (LaMDA-backed) - discussed and spot-checked qualitatively via illustrative examples (e.g., a hot-wiring instruction jailbreak, a Bing Chat webpage-injection scenario) rather than systematically benchmarked.
datasets_benchmarks: None - no standard or author-constructed benchmark dataset; the categorization draws on previously published prompt injection examples from the literature and the authors' own informal testing to verify or exclude questionable/undocumented cases.
key_result: No quantitative result is reported. The paper's main contribution is a qualitative categorization distinguishing direct and indirect prompt injection subtypes (e.g., double-character, virtualization/role-play, obfuscation, payload-splitting style attacks), illustrated with anecdotal examples such as a ChatGPT jailbreak eliciting hot-wiring instructions and a Bing Chat scenario where webpage content with hidden emoji-encoded instructions is executed.
baselines_compared: None - no defense method is proposed or compared against baselines; the paper is a categorization/survey with illustrative testing rather than a comparative evaluation.
threat_model: Direct prompt injection: an end user crafts creative input formatting (e.g., role-play framing) to bypass a chatbot interface's safety restrictions and elicit disallowed content. Indirect prompt injection: a third party embeds hidden instructions (e.g., invisible or encoded text) in external content such as a webpage, which an LLM-integrated tool (e.g., Bing Chat) later processes and executes as if it were a legitimate instruction, without the end user's awareness or intent.
stated_limitations: The authors state the categorization is not exhaustive since new prompt injection approaches are constantly emerging and they omitted questionable or single-source, undocumented examples found online; that most demonstrated prompt injections target only one or two LLM interfaces (predominantly ChatGPT/GPT-3/GPT-4), so generalization of specific examples to other chatbots is an assumption rather than a tested fact; and that they deliberately did not test indirect prompt injections against real systems to avoid ethical concerns about unaware third-party involvement.
technical_summary: Surveys the emerging threat of prompt injection against LLM-based chatbots and interfaces, proposing an early categorization that distinguishes direct prompt injection (an end user directly crafting input to bypass safety restrictions, e.g., jailbreak-style role-play) from indirect prompt injection (a third party embedding hidden instructions in external content later processed by the LLM tool, e.g., a poisoned webpage read by Bing Chat). Illustrates the categorization with anecdotal examples drawn from prior literature and informal testing rather than a systematic empirical evaluation, and discusses implications for LLM interface developers versus developers building services atop existing interfaces. Matters as an early, widely-cited attempt to organize the prompt-injection attack space into named subtypes, but it introduces no benchmark, no quantitative evaluation, and no defense of its own -- it is squarely a categorization/survey contribution.

title: Adversarial Attacks of Vision Tasks in the Past 10 Years: A Survey
artifacts_released: N - this is a survey with no code, dataset, or model release of its own.
models_evaluated: None directly evaluated by the authors; the survey discusses attacks and defenses reported by dozens of prior works against LVLMs including GPT-4V, LLaVA, and various CLIP-based and Transformer vision-language architectures.
datasets_benchmarks: None introduced; the survey references numerous prior LVLM safety benchmarks (e.g., RTVLM, SPA-VL, JailBreakV-28K, JailbreakHub) while explicitly noting the field still lacks a widely accepted, unified, comprehensive evaluation system.
key_result: No new empirical result; the survey's contribution is a unified taxonomy that classifies prompt injection, jailbreak, and cognitive-bias attacks on Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) under a common adversarial-attack paradigm distinguished by purpose (prompt injection is presented as the broadest concept, with jailbreak as its subset and indirect prompt injection identified by third-party rather than user-driven attacks), and it catalogs training-phase (adversarial fine-tuning, LoRA-based, prompt-tuning) and inference-phase (pre-processing defense prompts like AdaShield/SASP, post-processing detectors) defenses proposed across dozens of cited prior papers.
baselines_compared: None - as a survey it does not run its own comparative evaluation; it summarizes and organizes attack/defense comparisons reported in the surveyed primary papers.
threat_model: Synthesized across the surveyed literature: traditional adversarial-example attackers perturb visual inputs to fool classifiers; LVLM attackers additionally use prompt manipulation, typography-based image attacks, or cross-modal combinations to trigger jailbreaks (bypassing safety alignment, typically attacker=user) or prompt injection/indirect prompt injection (hijacking model output toward an attacker's goal, with the attacker often a third party embedding instructions in images or external content the LVLM later processes).
stated_limitations: The authors themselves note (as future directions, effectively limitations of the current field they survey) that text-modality attacks on LVLMs remain understudied relative to visual-modality attacks, that a widely accepted unified LVLM robustness benchmark is still lacking, that targeted-attack transferability lags far behind untargeted transferability, and that physically robust adversarial examples for LVLMs remain largely underexplored.
technical_summary: Surveys a decade of visual adversarial-attack research, covering both traditional (classification-focused) adversarial examples and the newer paradigm of attacks against Large Vision-Language Models, including prompt injection, jailbreaking, and cognitive-bias attacks. Proposes a unified categorization placing prompt injection, jailbreak, and cognitive bias under one adversarial-attack framework (with prompt injection as the broadest category and jailbreak as a subset), reviews attack techniques (prompt modification, adversarial perturbations, typography-based image attacks) and catalogs existing training-phase and inference-phase defenses (adversarial fine-tuning/LoRA, prompt-tuning, defense-prompt insertion methods like AdaShield, and post-hoc detectors). Matters to this corpus mainly for its treatment of cross-modal prompt injection and indirect prompt injection against LVLMs as part of a broader adversarial-ML lineage, but it is a pure survey/taxonomy contribution that introduces no new named attack, defense, or benchmark and no primary empirical evaluation.

title: PIGuard: Prompt Injection Guardrail via Mitigating Overdefense for Free
artifacts_released: Y - code and datasets released at https://github.com/leolee99/PIGuard
models_evaluated: PIGuard (author's model) versus baseline prompt guard models Fmops, Deepset, PromptGuard (Meta), LakeraGuard, LlamaGuard3, ProtectAIv2, and comparison against GPT-4o as a commercial LLM reference point
datasets_benchmarks: Introduces NotInject, a 339-sample over-defense evaluation dataset built from trigger words common in prompt injection attacks embedded in benign contexts (divided by trigger-word density); evaluates malicious accuracy using PINT and BIPIA benchmark attack data, benign accuracy using PINT and WildGuard benign data, and constructs an open-source training dataset combining existing malicious/benign corpora (e.g., Alpaca) with data-centric augmentation.
key_result: State-of-the-art prompt guard models (including ProtectAIv2) suffer severe over-defense, with over-defense accuracy on NotInject falling below 60% (near random guessing at 50%). PIGuard, trained with the proposed Mitigating Over-defense for Free (MOF) strategy, achieves 83.48% average accuracy across malicious, benign, and over-defense dimensions, surpassing the best prior open-source model (ProtectAIv2) by 30.4% (30.8% in the efficiency-adjusted table), with an over-defense accuracy of 87.32%, benign accuracy of 85.74%, and strong malicious accuracy, while rivaling commercial LLMs like GPT-4o and maintaining lower inference overhead than guardrail-style approaches.
baselines_compared: Fmops, Deepset, PromptGuard, LakeraGuard, LlamaGuard3, and ProtectAIv2 (the prior best open-source model) compared on malicious accuracy, benign accuracy, over-defense accuracy (via NotInject), average accuracy, and inference efficiency; an ablation isolating the contribution of data augmentation alone versus the full MOF training strategy is also reported.
threat_model: The defender operates a standalone prompt-guard classifier in front of an LLM application that must flag inputs containing prompt-injection instructions while not falsely flagging benign user inputs that merely contain trigger words (e.g., 'ignore') common in injection attacks; the paper's threat model centers on this over-defense failure mode of existing classifiers rather than on evaluating novel injection attack techniques.
stated_limitations: The authors state that although NotInject is carefully designed, it may not fully capture the diversity of real-world benign inputs, particularly in domain-specific applications such as healthcare or finance, potentially underestimating models' true over-defense tendency in those complex, sensitive domains, even though they consider the current dataset sufficient to reveal the over-defense problem broadly.
technical_summary: Identifies that existing prompt-injection guardrail models suffer from severe over-defense, falsely flagging benign inputs containing common injection trigger words (e.g., 'ignore') as malicious, and introduces NotInject, a 339-sample evaluation dataset systematically measuring this bias, showing state-of-the-art guard models' over-defense accuracy collapses to near-random levels. Proposes PIGuard, a new prompt guard model trained with a novel data-centric training strategy called Mitigating Over-defense for Free (MOF) that reduces trigger-word bias by curating and augmenting training data rather than adding inference-time cost. Evaluates on malicious accuracy (PINT, BIPIA), benign accuracy (PINT, WildGuard) and the new over-defense dimension (NotInject), showing PIGuard achieves state-of-the-art performance across all three simultaneously, outperforming the previous best open-source model by roughly 30 percentage points in average accuracy while remaining fully open-source. Matters as both a named diagnostic benchmark (NotInject) exposing a systemic weakness in prompt-injection detectors and a named, validated ingestion-stage detection defense (PIGuard/MOF) that directly fixes it.

title: Red Teaming the Mind of the Machine: A Systematic Evaluation of Prompt Injection and Jailbreak Vulnerabilities in LLMs
artifacts_released: N - no code, dataset, or model release; the 1,400+ prompt corpus is described as curated from public repositories but not itself released as a standalone artifact.
models_evaluated: GPT-4 (OpenAI, March 2024 snapshot), Claude 2 (Anthropic, July 2023 API), Mistral 7B (open-weight, via HF Inference), Vicuna-13B (via local HF inference server)
datasets_benchmarks: A curated corpus of 1,400+ adversarial prompts assembled from public jailbreak repositories (GitHub, JailbreakChat), LLM exploit forums (Reddit, Discord), and prior academic corpora including JailbreakBench and PromptBench, manually validated and categorized by attack type (roleplay, logic traps, encoding, multi-turn) and content sensitivity.
key_result: GPT-4 showed the highest attack success rate at 87.2%, followed by Claude 2 (82.5%), Mistral 7B (71.3%), and Vicuna (69.4%); roleplay-based prompts were the most effective attack category (89.6% ASR), followed by logic-trap (81.4%) and encoding-based (76.2%) attacks; jailbreaks that succeeded on GPT-4 transferred to Claude 2 and Vicuna in 64.1% and 59.7% of cases respectively, and average time-to-bypass ranged from about 16 to 22 minutes across models.
baselines_compared: The paper layers three existing external defenses (a PromptShield ruleset, a 'Palisade' detection framework, and Signed-Prompt verification logic) on top of successful jailbreaks to estimate defense coverage and bypass rate, rather than proposing or validating a new defense of its own; no quantitative bypass-rate results for these layered defenses are given in the extracted text beyond describing the retest methodology.
threat_model: A human red-teamer submits adversarial natural-language prompts (sourced from public jailbreak communities and academic corpora) directly to consumer-facing LLM APIs or locally hosted open-weight models, attempting to bypass built-in alignment/safety guardrails to elicit disallowed content (hate speech, illegal advice, malicious code) via techniques such as roleplay framing, logic traps, encoding obfuscation, and multi-turn context buildup; the attacker needs only standard API/chat access, no model internals.
stated_limitations: The authors state the study is limited by availability of open model weights and API constraints, that prompt injection tactics may evolve beyond what their dataset captures, that cultural/linguistic diversity in prompts is underrepresented (evaluation was English-centric), that static model checkpoints were used and may not reflect real-time moderation layers in production APIs, and that a shared, CVE-like collaborative tracking platform for prompt exploits and defense bypasses is needed as future work.
technical_summary: Conducts a systematic red-teaming evaluation of prompt injection and jailbreak vulnerabilities using a manually curated corpus of over 1,400 adversarial prompts (drawn from public exploit repositories, forums, and prior academic corpora) tested against four LLMs (GPT-4, Claude 2, Mistral 7B, Vicuna-13B) via a semi-automated LangChain-based pipeline scored with attack success rate, generalizability, time-to-bypass, and failure-mode classification metrics. Finds GPT-4 most vulnerable overall despite being most capable, roleplay-based attacks most effective across categories, and substantial cross-model transfer of successful jailbreaks; also layers three existing published defenses (PromptShield, a Palisade detector, Signed-Prompt) atop successful attacks to gauge coverage rather than introducing a new defense. Matters as a broad empirical cross-model vulnerability study and attack taxonomy, but proposes only general 'layered mitigation' recommendations rather than a new named, validated defense; the single-author study also relies on informal scoring methods (keyword spotting, GPT-based meta-evaluation) without released artifacts for independent verification.

title: Defending Against Prompt Injection With a Few DefensiveTokens
artifacts_released: Y - the paper states 'The code is available here' with a hyperlink whose URL text did not survive PDF extraction.
models_evaluated: Llama3-8B-Instruct, Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, Falcon3-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, each with and without DefensiveTokens, plus reproduced StruQ and SecAlign (LoRA and full fine-tuning variants) as training-time baselines and Reminder/Sandwich/an embedding-search baseline as test-time baselines
datasets_benchmarks: Cleaned Alpaca instruction-tuning dataset for training; AlpacaFarm and AlpacaEval2 (GPT-4o judge) for utility; five prompt injection security benchmarks including a >31K-sample manually-designed injection benchmark, the SEP benchmark (9.1K instruction/data/injection triples), GCG-based optimization attacks, and the InjecAgent agentic API-calling prompt injection benchmark.
key_result: On the largest benchmark (>31K samples), DefensiveToken reduces attack success rate to 0.24% averaged across four models, comparable to training-time defenses (0.20-0.51% ASR) and far below test-time baselines (over 11% ASR); against GCG optimization-based injection it lowers average ASR from 95.2% to 48.8%, versus about 70% ASR (with significant utility loss) for the strongest test-time baseline; on the InjecAgent agentic tool-calling benchmark it reduces average ASR 5x versus 2x for the best test-time baseline, all while imposing smaller utility loss than any baseline and allowing developers to skip the tokens entirely when utility is prioritized.
baselines_compared: Test-time defenses (Reminder, Sandwich, and a heuristic embedding-search baseline analogous to DefensiveToken but using discrete rather than optimized soft tokens) and training-time defenses (StruQ with LoRA and full fine-tuning, SecAlign with LoRA), all evaluated on the same five prompt-injection benchmarks and utility metrics.
threat_model: The user's instruction is benign, but application-retrieved external data (e.g., search results, tool outputs) contains an attacker-injected instruction that attempts to override the user's original task; attacks range from manually-designed optimization-free injections to strong GCG-style optimization-based injections and agentic tool-calling exploitation. The defense explicitly does not address settings where the user itself is malicious (jailbreaks, system-prompt extraction, data-exfiltration attacks).
stated_limitations: The authors state DefensiveToken only defends against prompt injection where the user is benign and external data is malicious, and does not apply to jailbreaks, system-prompt-following attacks, or data-extraction attacks where the user is the adversary; they also note utility was only measured via AlpacaEval2/AlpacaFarm and is not verified on a broader range of labeled utility datasets, and that learning-rate and token-insertion-position choices significantly affect the security-utility tradeoff, requiring careful tuning.
technical_summary: Proposes DefensiveToken, a test-time prompt-injection defense that inserts a small number (5, recommended) of newly added special tokens with embeddings optimized via a defensive instruction-tuning loss, similar to prompt tuning, so a system developer can prepend them before an LLM call to gain training-time-level security while retaining the option to drop them entirely and recover unmodified state-of-the-art utility when security is not a priority. Evaluates on four 7B/8B open-weight LLMs across five prompt-injection benchmarks spanning manually-designed, optimization-based (GCG), and agentic tool-calling attacks, and against both test-time and training-time defense baselines. Shows DefensiveToken approaches the security of full fine-tuning defenses like StruQ/SecAlign while imposing far less utility cost than any tested baseline, and vastly outperforms other test-time defenses. Matters as a lightweight, flexible defense that narrows the security-utility gap between prompting-based and fine-tuning-based prompt-injection defenses without requiring separate model deployments for secure versus high-utility use cases.

title: Goal-Guided Generative Prompt Injection Attack on Large Language Models
artifacts_released: N - no code, dataset, or availability statement appears in the extracted text.
models_evaluated: GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4-Turbo (gpt-4-0125-preview also used as an auxiliary sentence-generation model), Llama-2-7B, Llama-2-13B, Llama-2-70B (seven models total across two families)
datasets_benchmarks: 300 randomly sampled examples each from GSM8K, a web-based QA dataset, the MATH dataset, and SQuAD2.0; compared against mainstream black-box attack baselines (BertAttack, DeepWordBug, TextFooler, TextBugger, Prompt Bench, Semantic, CheckList) from Microsoft's Prompt Bench framework on SQuAD2.0 and MATH.
key_result: G2PIA, a query-free black-box attack that maximizes KL-divergence (equivalently Mahalanobis distance under a Gaussian assumption) between clean and adversarial text embeddings, achieves the highest attack success rate among compared methods on both SQuAD2.0 and MATH, notably 44.87% ASR on MATH versus BertAttack's 33.46%; ChatGPT-3.5 and Llama-2-7B show the weakest resistance among the seven tested models, ChatGPT-4-Turbo shows the strongest cross-model transferability of its generated attacks, and insertion position of the injected text has minimal impact on attack effectiveness.
baselines_compared: Mainstream black-box adversarial text attack methods from Microsoft's Prompt Bench (BertAttack, DeepWordBug, TextFooler, TextBugger, Prompt Bench, Semantic, CheckList), plus ablations against random breakpoint insertion and random sentence component replacement.
threat_model: A query-free black-box attacker (no access to victim model gradients or repeated querying) inserts a short generated adversarial text snippet into a clean question/context, aiming to maximize the KL-divergence between the LLM's output distribution on the clean versus adversarial input, thereby degrading task accuracy (e.g., on GSM8K, SQuAD2.0, MATH) without needing knowledge of the specific victim model's parameters.
stated_limitations: Not stated - the paper's conclusion section reiterates its theoretical contributions and reports strong attack transferability across models and datasets, but does not include an explicit statement of the method's own limitations or failure modes.
technical_summary: Introduces G2PIA (goal-guided generative prompt injection attack), a query-free black-box prompt injection attack that reframes the attack objective as maximizing the KL-divergence between the LLM's conditional output distributions on clean versus adversarial input, and proves this is equivalent to maximizing the Mahalanobis distance between their embedded representations under a Gaussian conditional-probability assumption. Uses an auxiliary LLM (GPT-4-Turbo) to generate constraint-satisfying injection text with low computational cost, requiring no victim-model queries or gradient access. Evaluates on seven LLMs (GPT-3.5/4-Turbo, Llama-2 7B/13B/70B) across four QA/math datasets, outperforming established black-box adversarial-text baselines (BertAttack, TextFooler, etc.) especially on the harder MATH dataset, and shows strong cross-model attack transferability. Matters as a theoretically-grounded, query-free black-box prompt injection attack technique that generalizes across task domains without task-specific tuning, but it proposes no defense of its own.
